That pushes the MT1 plug off the receptor, and the freed signal is designed to travel down to the FUS1 reporter. How the PAGER receptor is designed to

. How the PAGER receptor is designed to work. The yeast cell membrane is designed to carry an hM1Dq receptor whose extracellular recognition unit is an anti-H1N1 HA nanobody (Nb), while the MT1 inhibitor is designed to keep hM1Dq blocked whenever no antigen is present. When an influenza A (H1N1) HA antigen binds the na

fluenza A (H1N1) HA antigen binds the nanobody, the inhibitor is designed to be displaced from the receptor; with DCZ holding hM1Dq ready, the receptor is designed to hand the signal to the humanised Gα protein (the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Gpa1 C-terminus, last five residues changed from KIGII to EYNLV) and then to th

nged from KIGII to EYNLV) and then to the yeast MAPK cascade, where the FUS1 promoter drives the yEGFP or lacZ reporter. All of this is the intended design; no detection performance is claimed here. Future Vision: From H1N1 to the Broad Spectrum Platform PAGER-Yeast is designed to be antigen-agnostic: swap the recognit

o be antigen-agnostic: swap the recognition unit and the signal readout stays the same. The H1N1 prototype is the first instance of a platform rather than a single-purpose test — the same yeast, the same reporter, one new nanobody at a time. A wide target space Influenza A viruses carry 18 hemagglutinin and 11 neuramin

s carry 18 hemagglutinin and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1–H18, N1–N11) — every combination is a potential target for a swapped recognition unit (CDC, Types of Influenza Viruses, 2025). Modular recognition unit Keeping the α-factor secretion anchor and linker scaffold and swapping only the VHH sequence would extend cov

g only the VHH sequence would extend coverage toward H5, H7 and other subtypes, while the downstream GPCR signal rewiring and the dual-mode reporter stay universal. Field-ready readout Paired with a low-cost portable fluorescence reader, the same platform could serve primary-care screening, school morning checks and bo

screening, school morning checks and border quarantine ports. GER 可编程抗原门控受体技术将 HA 抗原识别事件转化为绿色荧光信号，构建低成本、高灵敏度的 POCT 生物传感器。 项目背景与动机 问题与潜在影响 流感作为全球重大公共卫生威胁，快速、准确的现场筛查是控制疫情传播的关键环节。现有临床检测方法存在以下局限： qRT-PCR：高准确度，但成本高、依赖专业实验设备、检测周期长，难以满足基层与现场需求。 ELISA：可高通量检测，但灵敏度偏低、孵育步骤复杂，对操作环境要求较高。 胶体金试纸条：操作简便、现场快速，但只能定性判读，低病毒载量样本易漏检。 上述方法在成本控制、灵敏度与便携性之间存在难以兼顾的矛盾，迫切需要开发一种低成本、高灵敏度、可现场部署的新型检测平台。 项目目标 本项目核

迫切需要开发一种低成本、高灵敏度、可现场部署的新型检测平台。 项目目标 本项目核心目标为：将 PAGER（Protein-fragment Assisted Interaction Reporter）可编程抗原门控受体技术应用于酿酒酵母，构建膜表面抗原识别融合蛋白，实现甲型流感病毒 HA 抗原的快速可视化检测。 当样本中存在 IAV HA 抗原时，酵母细胞表面的纳米抗体捕获抗原，通过空间位阻解除受体自抑制，在 DCZ 激动剂存在下激活下游 G 蛋白信号通路，驱动 FUS1 启动子表达 yEGFP/lacZ 报告基因，发出绿色荧光或蓝色显色信号，实现"抗原结合—荧光发光"的直接转换。 为何选择此项目 选择酿酒酵母作为生物传感器底盘基于

结合—荧光发光"的直接转换。 为何选择此项目 选择酿酒酵母作为生物传感器底盘基于以下考量：BY4741 遗传背景清晰、分子操作成熟、培养条件简单、生物安全等级为 BSL-1，适合规模化发酵生产。PAGER 系统将抗原识别与受体激活解耦，仅通过替换纳米抗体即可拓展至其他病原体检测，具有高度的模块化与可扩展性。 执行摘要：PAGER 策略通过"MT1 抑制肽—hM1Dq 受体—anti-HA 纳米抗体"三元嵌合设计实现抗原门控：无 HA 时通路关闭，有 HA 时空间位阻解除抑制并激活双模式报告系统。 核心设计思路：PAGER策略 抗原门控受体原理 PAGER（Protein-fragment Assisted Interaction R

（Protein-fragment Assisted Interaction Reporter，蛋白片段辅助互作报告系统）是一种基于空间位阻调控的可编程抗原门控受体策略。其核心是将抑制肽、抗原识别纳米抗体与 G 蛋白偶联受体（GPCR）整合为单一膜融合蛋白。 PAGER 膜融合蛋白结构（N→C 端） α-factor 信号肽 (GGGS)₃ MT1 抑制肽 (GGGS)₃ anti-HA 纳米抗体 (GGGS)₃ TEVcs Linker hM1Dq 受体 完整组装结构：α-factor-(GGGS)₃-MT1-(GGGS)₃-anti-HA-TEVcs-hM1Dq。柔性 (GGGS)₃ 接头作为空间延长臂，确保纳米抗体能够穿透酵母

-hM1Dq。柔性 (GGGS)₃ 接头作为空间延长臂，确保纳米抗体能够穿透酵母细胞壁孔隙并接触病毒颗粒抗原。 1 静息关闭状态 无 IAV HA 抗原时，MT1 抑制肽持续占据 hM1Dq 受体的正构位点，下游 G 蛋白级联被钳制在"关闭"状态，无荧光信号产生。 → 2 抗原识别与位阻解锁 HA 抗原与膜表面 anti-HA 纳米抗体结合，产生的空间位阻将 MT1 抑制肽从 hM1Dq 结合口袋中物理位移，解除自抑制。 → 3 DCZ 激活与信号输出 DCZ 小分子激动剂激活 hM1Dq，Gpa1-Gαq 嵌合蛋白触发 MAPK 通路，FUS1 启动子驱动 yEGFP/lacZ 表达，产生绿色荧光或蓝色显色。 双模式报告系统 项目

Motivation and Design Need EchoYeast requires a nanobody that specifically recognizes the hemagglutinin (HA) of influenza A (H1N1) virus with minimal cross-reactivity. We have 17 candidate nanobody sequences, but

ave 17 candidate nanobody sequences, but none of them have experimental structures in the PDB; moreover, screening them one by one by wet-lab experiments is both time-consuming and expensive. Therefore, the model must answer the following scientific questions: Among the 17 candidate nanobodies, which one has the optima

ate nanobodies, which one has the optimal binding ability and specificity for H1N1 HA? What is the binding mode between this nanobody and H1N1 HA? What are the key hotspot residues? e? Which candidates should be prioritized for wet-lab experiments? Which should be eliminated? We adopt a computational-first / model-guided strategy, using multiscale computational models to guide experimental design rather than replace experiments. 2. est Plan. Problem Statement Waiting for someone to run a fever Influenza A virus (IAV) is a persistent global public-health threat. WHO estimates that seasonal influenza causes around 1 billion infections, 3–5 million cases of severe illness and 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths each year, with children, older adults

each year, with children, older adults and immunocompromised people carrying the heaviest burden [1]. The surface haemagglutinin (HA) protein continually escapes existing population immunity through antigenic drift and shift, so vaccine strains always lag behind circulating strains: the virus keeps changing, while our

ins: the virus keeps changing, while our window on it opens only once symptoms appear. Starting from symptoms decides what such a chain can and cannot record. A throat swab can only be taken from someone already feverish or coughing; before that point, the particles they exhale are already in the air of the same room.

re already in the air of the same room. This is not speculation: air-sampling studies have recovered influenza A virus RNA from indoor air in a health centre and a day-care centre, at total concentrations of 5.8×10³–3.7×10⁴ genome copies per cubic metre, with about 64% of the viral load carried on fine particles below

al load carried on fine particles below 2.5 µm that can stay suspended for hours [2]. Patient-centred surveillance therefore carries a built-in delay — it records what has happened, and does not announce what is about to. The half that travels through the air Bringing air into the picture is what closes that gap. The m

e picture is what closes that gap. The most direct gain is pre-symptomatic warning: detecting virus in indoor air before large numbers of clinical cases appear gives control measures a head start — ventilation, disinfection and crowd management can be scheduled before infections happen rather than after. It also puts r

happen rather than after. It also puts risk in its proper place. Within one building, classrooms, wards and waiting halls do not carry the same risk, and air monitoring can tell which zones are the hot spots, so that limited effort goes where it is needed. For national influenza networks, built around clinical patients

networks, built around clinical patients, this adds the environmental dimension that trend assessment currently lacks. And in the settings that carry the heaviest burden — schools and care homes — a real-time air risk assessment bears directly on reducing cluster outbreaks. Diluted almost to the point of disappearing F

Viral particles occur at very low concentration in ambient air, and a sampler can process only a limited volume of it; multiply the two and what reaches

f it; multiply the two and what reaches the liquid is a very small amount indeed. The accepted paradigm is a two-step workflow: a bioaerosol sampler collects airborne particles on site, and the sample is then sent back to a central laboratory for qRT-PCR. It is sensitive and dependable, but it splits sampling from dete

ndable, but it splits sampling from detection across two places and two moments, with transport and laboratory turnaround in between, so what comes back is usually retrospective data rather than a field result [3]. Sampling itself also loses material: the collection efficiency of cyclone samplers varies widely with des

cyclone samplers varies widely with design and falls at high flow rates as the collection liquid evaporates and already-captured particles are re-aerosolised [4]. No mature low-cost option exists for on-site airborne IAV detection — that gap is what we set out to fill. Choosing what emits the signal The next question

what emits the signal The next question is what should emit the signal. The familiar answer is a chemical reagent: a chromogenic substrate, an antibody, an enzyme label. That led us to change how the signal is generated: instead of an added colour reaction or an antibody, we let a living cell report what it has sensed. Handing the amplification to the cell The most substantive advantage of using yeast is that recogni

advantage of using yeast is that recognition and amplification can happen inside one cell. The recognition element is a genetically encoded protein: the anti-HA nanobody is carried on a plasmid and copied along with the cell, so every yeast cell produces its own reagent and no antibody cold chain or batch comparison is

One receptor activated by one antigen is turned, through the GPCR–MAPK cascade, into transcription of a large amount of fluorescent protein from the FUS1 promoter — a classic strongly pheromone-inducible promoter [11] — a level of

To turn antigen binding into gene expression, three changes at the ge

The first releases the pathway's own brake: knocking out FAR1 and SST2 removes the G1 cell-cycle arrest and the negative regulation imposed by the mating pheromone pathway, so that the signal can be sustained and stable [6]. How We Got Here: From Wet-Cyclone Collection to a Cup of Glowing Medium This hardware began with a concrete observation. While reading up on how airborne bioaerosols are sampled, we came across the

aerosols are sampled, we came across the wet-cyclone principle: air is spun at high speed inside a chamber, aerosol particles are driven to the wall by centrifugal force, captured by a liquid film on that wall, and end up as liquid in a collection cup. The technique exists in order to collect what is in the air and han

er to collect what is in the air and hand it on for later analysis. We paused there. If the endpoint of collection is a cup of liquid anyway, why should that liquid only ever be water or buffer? If we replace the collection liquid with medium containing our yeast, sampling and detection can happen in the same cup. How

tection can happen in the same cup. How the process runs Following that thought, the whole process falls into eight steps: The device draws in air, and the cyclone spins airborne particles — including any influenza A virus present — into the liquid in the cup. That liquid is our engineered yeast culture, and the yeast

engineered yeast culture, and the yeast cells carry the PAGER fusion receptor on their surface, whose nanobody domain recognises the HA protein on the influenza A virion. When HA binds the nanobody, steric hindrance displaces the auto-inhibitory peptide MT1 from the hM1Dq receptor, relieving the receptor's self-inhibit

r, relieving the receptor's self-inhibition. In the presence of the agonist DCZ, which is already in the cup with the yeast before sampling starts, the de-repressed receptor activates the yeast MAPK pathway through the Gpa1–Gαq chimeric G protein, and the FUS1 promoter is switched on. FUS1 drives transcription of yEGFP

d on. FUS1 drives transcription of yEGFP, and the yeast begins to synthesise green fluorescent protein. We shine 485 nm excitation light into the sampling cup, exciting the fluorescent protein that has already been expressed. The fluorescent protein emits at 528 nm, collected by a receiver placed at 90° in space to the

a receiver placed at 90° in space to the excitation path. The receiver converts the optical signal into an electrical signal, and from that signal we judge whether influenza A virus is present in this air sample. The 90° angle is not arbitrary. The excitation beam is strong and the fluorescence is weak, and their centr

he fluorescence is weak, and their centre wavelengths differ by only about 43 nm. If the receiver sat on the same axis as the emitter, scattered excitation light would simply swamp the fluorescence. Turning it 90° takes the main excitation beam out of the receiver's direction, and two narrow-band filters then separate

d two narrow-band filters then separate that 43 nm properly. One more point is worth stating. DCZ sits in the same liquid as the yeast from before sampling begins, so the switch of this system is in practice thrown by HA alone: without HA the receptor stays self-inhibited and the pathway is closed, and only when HA is

pathway is closed, and only when HA is present is that inhibition relieved. DCZ effectively presets the switch to a state in which it can be opened, and the discriminating signal comes from the antigen itself. The three blocks in the hardware The hardware therefore falls into three blocks, each matching one stretch of

ree blocks, each matching one stretch of that flow: the heated block keeps the yeast at its optimum 30 °C; the detachable optical plugs provide the 485 nm excitation and 528 nm collection paths; and the signal-acquisition circuit turns the nanoampere-to-microampere photocurrent from the photodiode into a number we can

rom the photodiode into a number we can act on. Design Goals and Constraints Temperature: yeast protein expression and signalling are temperature sensitive, and drift directly changes the amplitude of the fluorescence signal. Control accuracy is therefore specified as ±0.5 °C with a set point of 30 °C. Optics: yEGFP is

h a set point of 30 °C. Optics: yEGFP is a codon-optimised green fluorescent protein reporter for yeast, conventionally excited with blue light (about 485 nm) and read out in the green channel (about 528 nm) [12], only ~43 nm apart. Narrow-band filters (30 nm FWHM, OD3) are required to separate excitation from emission

red to separate excitation from emission, and the excitation and collection axes are placed at 90° to suppress direct excitation breakthrough geometrically. Sample volume: ≥ 1.5 mL at the cuvette stage; at the collection-cup stage the cup is pre-filled with 20 mL of medium containing the yeast, which brings the liquid

ning the yeast, which brings the liquid level just above the junction between the cone and the cylinder. Light sealing: we measure microampere-level photocurrent from a photodiode, and ambient light is the dominant noise source. Light sealing is therefore a structural requirement rather than an accessory. Serviceabilit
